corrected_text: The shape of the chest in the Mammalia varies in general as the clavicles are present or wanting. In animals provided with clavicles, as the Quadrumana, bats, the squirrel, beaver, mole, ant-eater, hedgehog, and sloth, the shape of the chest approaches to the human, or is conical, and flattened before and behind. In those void of clavicles it is compressed laterally, from the smaller incurvation of the ribs; and the sternum makes a remarkable prominence, so that the transverse or intercostal diameter is less proportionally, and the sterno-vertebral is greater proportionally, than in man and the claviculated animals. In the long-legged animals, as the giraffe and those of the stag kind, this prominence of the sternum is sufficient to give it a keel-like appearance (thorax carinatus). In the carnivorous animals the chest presents its greatest longitudinal extent.
